title: Acute migraine attack (adult)
subject: neurology
summary: Screen for secondary headache red flags, then treat in the ED with IV prochlorperazine or metoclopramide, an NSAID (ketorolac or dexketoprofen) or SC sumatriptan, consider a greater occipital nerve block, give dexamethasone to reduce recurrence, and avoid opioids.

sections.title: Confirm migraine and look for red flags
items: Migraine: recurrent attacks lasting 4 to 72 hours, often unilateral and pulsating, moderate to severe, worse with activity, with nausea or light and sound sensitivity; some patients have aura.

Red flags needing imaging or LP: thunderclap onset, new headache after 50, fever or neck stiffness, focal deficit, papilloedema, altered consciousness, seizure, pregnancy or postpartum, cancer or immunosuppression, positional headache, trauma, progressive or changed pattern.
Status migrainosus: a debilitating attack lasting more than 72 hours.
Do not attribute first-ever aura with weakness, or aura starting after age 50, to migraine until TIA and stroke are excluded.

sections.title: Emergency department treatment (AHS 2025)
items: First line: prochlorperazine 10 mg IV (must offer) or metoclopramide 10 mg IV (should offer), infused over about 15 minutes to reduce akathisia; IV fluids if dehydrated.
Add an NSAID: ketorolac 30 mg IV (15 mg if age 65 or over, weight below 50 kg or renal impairment) or dexketoprofen 50 mg IV (available in India).
Sumatriptan 6 mg SC if there is no vascular contraindication and no triptan or ergot in the previous 24 hours.
Greater occipital nerve block with local anaesthetic (must offer, AHS 2025) where trained staff are available.
To reduce recurrence after discharge: dexamethasone 10 mg IV once (AHS 2016 should offer; 2025 update may offer).
Refractory: chlorpromazine 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 25 mg) with a fluid bolus, or sodium valproate 500 to 1000 mg IV (not in pregnancy or women who could become pregnant).
Do not give hydromorphone (must not offer) or other opioids; IV paracetamol is not recommended as ED treatment.

sections.title: Outpatient acute treatment
items: Treat early in the attack. Offer an oral triptan with an NSAID or paracetamol, and consider an antiemetic (metoclopramide 10 mg or domperidone 10 mg orally) even without nausea (NICE).
Sumatriptan 50 to 100 mg orally; a second dose after at least 2 hours only if the headache returns (max 200 mg in 24 hours). Rizatriptan 10 mg (5 mg if taking propranolol), max 20 mg in 24 hours.
Single-drug options: ibuprofen 400 mg, naproxen 500 mg, aspirin 900 mg or paracetamol 1000 mg orally.
Triptan contraindications: coronary, cerebrovascular or peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic or brainstem aura.
If at least 2 triptans fail or triptans are contraindicated: a gepant (rimegepant 75 mg orally, max 1 dose in 24 hours) or lasmiditan where available (AHS 2021).

Limit acute treatment days: triptans, opioids, ergots or combination analgesics on 10 or more days a month, or simple analgesics on 15 or more days a month for 3 months, cause medication overuse headache.
Do not offer opioids or ergots for migraine (NICE).

sections.title: Pregnancy and older adults
items: Pregnancy: paracetamol first; metoclopramide is acceptable; a triptan or NSAID may be considered after discussion, but avoid NSAIDs in the third trimester and prolonged use after 20 weeks. Avoid valproate and ergots.
New or changed headache in pregnancy or postpartum: exclude pre-eclampsia (BP, urine protein), cerebral venous thrombosis, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction and pituitary apoplexy.
New headache after age 50: check ESR and CRP (giant cell arteritis) and image; use triptans and NSAIDs cautiously because of vascular and renal risk.

sections.title: Discharge and follow-up
items: Discharge when pain is controlled, oral fluids are tolerated and the neurological examination is normal. Warn about drowsiness and akathisia; no driving after sedating treatment.
Give a written plan: treat early, triptan plus NSAID, antiemetic, and limits on acute medication days.
Refer for preventive treatment if attacks are frequent or disabling or acute medication use is high.
Admit for status migrainosus refractory to ED treatment, dehydration, or diagnostic uncertainty.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Assuming migraine because pain improved with treatment: SAH, cerebral venous thrombosis, meningitis, carbon monoxide poisoning and hypertensive emergency can also improve.
Using opioids: more recurrence, medication overuse headache and return visits.
Not recognising akathisia or acute dystonia after dopamine antagonists; treat with diphenhydramine 25 mg IV or promethazine 25 mg IM.
Giving a triptan to a patient with vascular disease or within 24 hours of ergotamine.
Missing medication overuse headache in frequent ED attenders.

drugs.name: Prochlorperazine
drugs.notes: AHS 2025 must offer. Akathisia, dystonia, sedation.

drugs.name: Metoclopramide
drugs.dose: 10 mg IV over about 15 minutes, once
drugs.notes: AHS should offer. Oral 10 mg as antiemetic at home.

drugs.name: Ketorolac
drugs.dose: 30 mg IV once (15 mg if age 65 or over, under 50 kg or renal impairment)
drugs.notes: Avoid with GI bleeding, significant renal impairment, third trimester.

drugs.name: Dexketoprofen
drugs.notes: AHS 2025 should offer. Same NSAID cautions.

drugs.name: Sumatriptan
drugs.dose: 6 mg SC once (ED); or 50 to 100 mg orally, may repeat after 2 hours if recurrence, max 200 mg in 24 hours
drugs.notes: Contraindicated in coronary, cerebrovascular or peripheral vascular disease and uncontrolled hypertension.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.notes: Reduces headache recurrence after ED discharge.

drugs.name: Chlorpromazine
drugs.dose: 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 25 mg) with fluid bolus

drugs.name: Sodium valproate
drugs.notes: Refractory attacks. Not in pregnancy or women who could become pregnant; avoid in liver disease.
